{{Short description|none}}
The [[governor of Massachusetts]] is the [[head of government]] of [[Massachusetts]]. Since 1780, 65 people have been elected governor, six to non-consecutive terms ([[John Hancock]], [[Caleb Strong]], [[Marcus Morton]], [[John Davis (Massachusetts politician)|John Davis]], [[John A. Volpe]], and [[Michael Dukakis]]), and seven [[Lieutenant Governor of Massachusetts|lieutenant governors]] have acted as governor without subsequently being elected governor. [[Thomas Talbot (Massachusetts politician)|Thomas Talbot]] served a stint as acting governor, but was elected governor several years later. Prior to 1918 constitutional reforms, both the governor's office and that of lieutenant governor were vacant on one occasion, when the state was governed by the [[Massachusetts Governor's Council|Governor's Council]].

==List of governors==
===Colonial Massachusetts===
{{Further|List of colonial governors of Massachusetts}}
The colonial history of Massachusetts begins with the founding first of the [[Plymouth Colony]] in 1620, and then the [[Massachusetts Bay Colony]] in 1628. The [[Dominion of New England]] combined these and other [[New England]] colonies into a single unit in 1686, but collapsed in 1689. In 1692 the [[Province of Massachusetts Bay]] was established, merging Plymouth and Massachusetts Bay, which then included the territory of present-day [[Maine]].

Colonial governors of Plymouth and the Massachusetts Bay Colony were elected annually by a limited subset of the male population (known as [[freeman (Thirteen Colonies)|freemen]]), while Dominion officials and those of the 1692 province were appointed by the British crown. In 1774 General [[Thomas Gage]] became the last royally appointed governor of Massachusetts. He was recalled to England after the [[Battle of Bunker Hill]] in June 1775, by which time the [[Massachusetts Provincial Congress]] exercised ''de facto'' control of Massachusetts territory outside British-occupied [[Boston]]. Between 1775 and the establishment of the [[Constitution of Massachusetts|Massachusetts State Constitution]] in 1780 the state was governed by the provincial congress and an executive council.

===Commonwealth of Massachusetts: 1780–present===
The constitution of Massachusetts created the offices of governor{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-50425 1780 pt. 1, chp. II, § I, art. I]}} and lieutenant governor,{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-50473 1780 pt. 1, chp. II, § II, art. I]}} to be elected annually.{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-50427 1780 pt. 1, chp. II, § I, art. II]}} Terms were lengthened to two years in 1918, to last until their successor was inaugurated, which would be at least the first Wednesday in the January after their election.{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-53543 1918 amend. LXIV]}} This was changed to the Thursday following the first Wednesday in the January after the election in 1950,{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-53816 1950 amend. LXXX]}} and terms were lengthened to four years in 1964.{{sfn|Mass. Const.|loc=[https://50constitutions.org/ma/constitution/section-id-53820 1964 amend. LXXXII]}}
